subsection: 2. O'Connell after 1829, the Tithe War, the Poor Law and Young Ireland, 1830–1848

notes.h: O'Connell at Westminster and the Whig alliance
notes.b: After taking his seat in 1830, O'Connell worked with the Whig government for reform in Ireland, trading support for concessions.
points: O'Connell was re-elected for County Clare in 1830 and took his seat in the House of Commons, having been unable to do so in 1829 because of the oath.
He supported the Whig government of Earl Grey, which passed the Reform Act of 1832 and reduced the restrictions on the franchise in Britain and Ireland.
The Lichfield House Compact of 1835 was an informal understanding between O'Connell and the Whig leaders, under which the Whigs promised reforms in return for Irish Liberal support.
Lord Mulgrave was appointed Lord Lieutenant in 1835, and his Under-Secretary Thomas Drummond ran a reform-minded administration in Dublin until 1840.
The Municipal Corporations (Ireland) Act of 1840 reformed the corporations of Irish towns and opened them to Catholic councillors and voters.
O'Connell was elected Lord Mayor of Dublin in 1841, the first Catholic to hold the office since the seventeenth century.

notes.b: Repeal of the Union was O'Connell's main aim after 1830, and the campaign used mass meetings to press it on the British government.
points: The Repeal Association was founded in Dublin in 1840, with O'Connell as its leader and a membership fee that made it a mass movement.
The 'Repeal Year' of 1843 saw a series of monster meetings, large open-air gatherings held across Ireland, many attended by hundreds of thousands of people.
The government at Westminster, under Robert Peel, responded by prosecuting O'Connell and other leaders for conspiracy to hold illegal assemblies.
O'Connell cancelled a planned monster meeting at Clontarf, near Dublin, in October 1843 after the government banned it and troops were drafted into the city.
He was arrested in October 1843 and convicted in 1844 of conspiracy, with a sentence of imprisonment; the House of Lords overturned the convictions in September 1844.
Contemporary opinion was divided: Protestant opinion saw Repeal as a threat to the Union and to property, while many Catholics saw the campaign as the means of securing Irish self-government.
Historians have argued that the Repeal campaign failed because Westminster would not concede a separate parliament, and because O'Connell refused to countenance physical force.

notes.h: The Young Ireland split and O'Connell's death
notes.b: The Young Ireland movement challenged O'Connell's leadership and split the Repeal movement in 1846.
points: Young Ireland was the name given to a group of writers and activists who wrote for The Nation, a weekly newspaper founded in Dublin in October 1842.
The Nation was edited by Charles Gavan Duffy, with John Blake Dillon and Thomas Davis among its leading contributors.
The Young Irelanders wanted a broader nationalism that drew on Irish history, literature and language rather than on the Catholic campaign alone.
The peace resolutions of 1846 were passed by the Repeal Association, in response to Young Ireland's advocacy of force, and they committed the movement to non-violence.
The Young Irelanders, led by John Mitchel and others, left the Association after the peace resolutions and formed the Irish Confederation in 1847.
O'Connell died at Genoa in May 1847 while travelling to Rome, and his death ended the mass Repeal movement he had led.

notes.b: Tithes, paid to the Church of Ireland by Catholic and dissenting tenant farmers, sparked a campaign of non-payment and violent resistance in the 1830s.
points: Tithe was a tax paid to the established Church of Ireland, although most of the population who paid it were Catholic.
Tithe disputes were fought out in the countryside, where tithe proctors seized goods or livestock to recover arrears.
The campaign of non-payment and resistance became known as the Tithe War and reached its height between 1831 and 1836.
Carrickshock in County Kilkenny in December 1831 was a notable clash, in which a group of tithe process servers and their police escort were attacked and several men were killed.
The government used troops and police to protect tithe collection, and many tithe proctors were attacked in return.
The Tithe Rentcharge Act of 1838 converted tithes into a rent charge paid by the landlord, which removed the tithe from the tenant farmer and ended the main source of conflict.

notes.b: The Irish Poor Law of 1838 introduced a system of workhouses financed by a rate on property, after a commission's proposals were rejected.
points: The Archbishop of Dublin, Richard Whately, chaired a royal commission in the 1830s, and its proposals were rejected by the government in favour of a system based on the English model.
George Nicholls, who had helped to introduce the English Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834, was sent to Ireland to report on the operation of relief in the country.
The Irish Poor Law Act of 1838 divided the country into unions, each run by a board of guardians elected by ratepayers.
Each union had a workhouse, where the destitute were admitted under the workhouse test, which was intended to deter all but the most desperate.
The poor rate was levied on the valuation of property, and landlords were liable to pay it, which gave them a direct financial interest in the system.
The system was designed to provide relief for the destitute, not to relieve general distress, and it was still in operation when the Famine began in 1845.

notes.h: Young Ireland's writers and the cultural nationalism of The Nation
notes.b: The Nation's writers tried to build a national identity that could include Protestants and Catholics, drawing on history, poetry and ballads.
points: Thomas Davis, the most influential of the Young Irelanders, wrote essays and poems for The Nation under the pseudonym The Celt.
The Nation published songs and ballads that celebrated Irish history and the Irish people, and many became popular in homes and at public gatherings.
Davis argued that Irish nationality should be based on a common culture and history, not on religion, and he invited Protestants to join the nation.
The Irish Confederation, founded in 1847, brought together Young Irelanders and others who opposed O'Connell's continued adherence to constitutional methods.
The Young Irelanders' cultural nationalism prepared the ground for later movements in the language, literature and sport of the country, though its direct political results were small.

notes.b: The Young Irelanders' attempt at armed rebellion in 1848 was small in scale and collapsed within days.
points: The rising of 1848 followed the revolutions in France and Europe earlier that year, and the Young Irelanders hoped that Irish peasants would join them.
William Smith O'Brien led the rising, which took place near the village of Ballingarry in County Tipperary in late July 1848.
The rising ended on 29 July 1848 when a small group of rebels was dispersed by police at a farmhouse in Ballingarry.
The rebellion failed because the rural population did not join it, the Catholic Church opposed it, and the police and troops were ready.
Smith O'Brien, Thomas Francis Meagher, Terence MacManus and Patrick O'Donohoe were sentenced to be hanged for high treason, and the sentences were commuted to transportation to Van Diemen's Land.

notes.b: Davis was the leading intellectual of Young Ireland, and his writing shaped later ideas of nationality.
points: Thomas Davis was born in 1814 in Mallow, County Cork, to a Protestant family, and he studied at Trinity College Dublin, where he trained as a barrister.
He co-founded The Nation in October 1842 with Charles Gavan Duffy and John Blake Dillon, and he was its main ideological voice until his death.
He argued that the nation was a community of people sharing a common culture, history and language, and he regarded the Irish language as a central part of that culture.
His main action was the cultural and literary campaign carried out through The Nation, not a political organisation or a military role.
Davis was a participant in the Repeal movement and a supporter of Repeal until the peace resolutions of 1846, but he was not a leader of the Repeal Association.
He died of scarlet fever in September 1845, aged 30, before the Famine's full impact and before the 1848 rising.
Contemporaries saw him as a gifted and idealistic writer, and his poems and ballads were sung widely; his radicalism was more controversial among moderate nationalists.
Later historians have stressed his attempt to build a national identity across religious lines, while noting that his inclusive vision was weakened by sectarian divisions after his death.

notes.b: Judgements of O'Connell's leadership depend on whether the test is Emancipation and reform, or the Repeal of the Union.
points: Achievement: Emancipation was won in 1829, and in the 1830s he helped secure municipal reform and reform of the Irish corporations.
Limit: Repeal of the Union was not achieved, and the Repeal Association was defeated in the 1843 crisis without any government concession on a separate parliament.
Achievement: O'Connell built a mass political movement with a mass membership and an organised system of collections, meetings and newspapers.
Limit: the movement depended on his personal leadership, and it split in 1846 when Young Ireland refused to accept his opposition to force.
Contemporary view: many Catholics saw him as the Liberator who had brought them into politics, and Protestant critics saw him as a demagogue who threatened the Union.
Later view: historians have judged his legacy by the scale of his organisation and by the limits of constitutional methods in achieving self-government.

keyTerms.definition: The campaign to dissolve the Union and restore an Irish Parliament in Dublin, led by O'Connell through the Repeal Association from 1840.
A community bound by shared history, culture and language, which the Young Irelanders, especially Thomas Davis, used to define Irish nationality.
The belief that Irish independence could be won only by armed rebellion, which Young Ireland's advocates of force argued for and the peace resolutions of 1846 rejected.
A tax paid to the established Church of Ireland, the non-payment of which caused the Tithe War of the 1830s.
An 1835 understanding between O'Connell and the Whig leaders, under which Irish Liberal support was exchanged for reforms.
A large open-air gathering held during the Repeal campaign, particularly in 1843, to show popular support for Repeal.
An institution established under the Irish Poor Law Act of 1838, where destitute people were housed and given relief in return for work.
The elected body in each poor law union that ran the workhouse and administered relief under the 1838 Poor Law.

factCards.definition: An informal understanding between O'Connell and the Whig leaders in 1835, under which the Whigs promised reform in return for Irish Liberal support.
The mass movement founded in Dublin in 1840, under O'Connell, to campaign for the repeal of the Union.
O'Connell cancelled a planned monster meeting at Clontarf in October 1843 after the government banned it and troops were sent into Dublin.
Resolutions passed by the Repeal Association in 1846 committing the movement to peaceful methods, which led to the Young Ireland split.
A weekly founded in Dublin in October 1842 by Davis, Duffy and Dillon, which became the main voice of Young Ireland.
A clash in County Kilkenny in December 1831 in which tithe process servers and their escort were attacked and several men killed during the Tithe War.
The Act that converted tithes into a rent charge paid by the landlord, ending the tithe as a tenant farmers' grievance.
The Act that divided Ireland into poor law unions, each with a workhouse and a board of guardians elected by ratepayers.
The movement formed by the Young Irelanders after they left the Repeal Association, which aimed at a broader nationalism.
The small rising led by William Smith O'Brien in County Tipperary in July 1848, which was dispersed by police within a day.
O'Connell died at Genoa in May 1847 while travelling to Rome, ending his leadership of the mass Repeal movement.
The Young Ireland writer and co-founder of The Nation, who died of scarlet fever in September 1845.
